cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and Tocklai clones, with some Chinary plantings at higher altitude
processing: Fully oxidised black tea from young estates and smallholders, made both CTC and orthodox; the orthodox spring and second-flush lots are the ones with character, and a few makers also produce green and white tea.
harvest_season: March to November, with spring and second-flush lots the most interesting.
appearance_dry: Dark, twisted leaf with some golden tips.
taste_profile: Between Assam and the hill teas: malty and honeyed with a touch of fruit and a brisk but not heavy finish.

brewing.notes: Just under the boil, 3–4 minutes, milk optional; orthodox leaf gives a second steep.

vintage_note: Sold mostly through the Guwahati auction as part of the north-eastern crop and, in small quantities, as single-garden lots by flush and year from speciality sellers (Donyi Polo Tea Estate, run by the state, is the name most often seen). Production is small and growing; buy the current season's lot and use within a year or two.
description:
Arunachal Pradesh, the big, thinly populated state in India's far north-east, is one of the country's youngest tea regions: a few estates were planted in the foothills in the closing decades of the twentieth century, and smallholder gardens have followed. Most of it is Assam-type bush grown at low altitude, so the teas sit between Assam and the hill teas, but a handful of makers have pushed into orthodox and speciality styles and started to get noticed.

Manufacture follows the Assam pattern, with both CTC and orthodox factories: wither, roll, full oxidation and firing. The orthodox lots, often from the spring and second flush, are the ones with character; some growers also make green and white tea in small amounts.

The cup is red-amber, malty and honeyed with a touch of fruit and a brisk but not heavy finish; think of a softer, slightly brighter Assam. Brew it with water just under the boil for three to four minutes, with or without milk, and expect a second steep from orthodox leaf.

It is sold mostly through the Guwahati auction as part of the north-eastern crop and, in small quantities, as single-garden lots by flush and year from speciality sellers; Donyi Polo Tea Estate is the garden you are most likely to see named. Production is small and growing. Buy the current season's lot and use within a year or two.

An interesting one to taste next to an Assam from the same year: same bush, different hills.
sources_note: Arunachal's tea industry is young and documentation is thin; planting dates and the Donyi Polo estate details are from memory. No Wikipedia article on Arunachal tea.
